Need to search first.I ran out of search and fetch requests partway through, so these notes cover less ground than you asked for. Everything below comes from search-result extracts of a few verse-by-verse pages. I found nothing for Catholic or Orthodox readings, nothing on differences between the Protestant traditions, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Those sections are left out.

## 2 Chronicles 2: Research notes

**v. 1**
- In Hebrew "purposed" (KJV "determined") is literally "said." Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary note this. Keil & Delitzsch say that with an infinitive after it, the word means "to plan to do something," not "to command." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/2-1.htm
- Pulpit: "the Name of the LORD" stands for God himself. "A house for his kingdom" (KJV) means Solomon's royal palace. Gill: the temple came first and the palace after, and they were built in that order. Same URL.
- Guzik: for the Chronicler, the temple matters more than Solomon's wisdom or wealth. That is why it skips parts of Kings that are told there. The point spoke to returning exiles who were rebuilding their own temple. He cites Selman. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-2/
- JFB: the temple is the main subject here, and the palace is mentioned only in passing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/2-2.htm

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: "told out" means counted out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/2-2.htm
- Guzik takes these men to be Canaanite slave labourers and the 3,600 to be middle managers. He quotes Selman: 1 Kings 5:16 gives 3,300, but the Greek (LXX) text of Kings is uncertain there, and Chronicles may keep the better number. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-2/
- Geneva Bible notes: 3,600 counts every kind of officer, while the chief officers numbered 3,300 as in 1 Kings 5:16. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/2-2.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik: Solomon's appeal rests on David's good relations with Hiram, which shows David did not treat every neighbouring nation as an enemy. Hiram is short for Ahiram ("my brother is exalted"). Josephus said copies of these letters still existed in his day. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-2/
- JFB: the letters were probably written on both sides (see v. 11). The wording suggests this Huram was the same king who had been David's friend. Gill: in 1 Kings, Hiram first sent congratulations, which Chronicles leaves out. Cambridge: Huram is the same name as Hiram, and Menander puts his reign at 34 years. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/2-3.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: Chronicles drops the congratulatory embassy because it did not matter to the negotiations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/2-1.htm

**vv. 4–5**
- Matthew Henry: Solomon tries to give Huram "great and high thoughts" of Israel's God. Believers should take every chance to speak of God to others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_chronicles/2.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: the temple has to be great because the LORD is greater than all gods (Exod. 18:11; Deut. 10:17). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/2-6.htm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: Solomon knows God cannot be housed in a building. He builds for God's worship, not as God's home. The "sacrifice" here literally means incense, used in a general sense. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/2-6.htm
- Benson, Poole, Gill and Matthew Henry all say the temple was not meant to contain the infinite God, unlike the "temples made with hands" of other nations (Acts 17:24). It was a fitting place for priests and worshippers. Barnes: the reason for the temple lies on the human side, not God's. Geneva: no one can honour God as perfectly as his majesty deserves. Same URL, and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/2-6.html
- Clarke cites the Jewish Targum, which speaks of lower, middle and upper heavens, none of which can hold God. Coffman denies that Old Testament believers thought God could be boxed in. Smith: trying to "localize" God is always wrong (Ps. 139). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/2-6.html
- Guzik, quoting Morgan and Trapp: by the standards of the pagans of his day, Solomon's idea of God was biblical and high. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-2/
- The BibleHub Study Bible links "highest heavens" to the ancient idea of several layers of heaven. https://biblehub.com/study/2_chronicles/2-6.htm

**vv. 7–9**
- Guzik: Solomon used foreign craftsmen and timber because he wanted the best, so the temple was not built for Israel alone. Payne says Israel's building skills lagged behind its northern neighbours, and archaeology shows rougher-cut stone. Dilday says the Sidonians were famous for timber work. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-2/
- Preacher's Homiletical: v. 7 is a call for people to devote their skills to God's work. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/2-12.html

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: "beaten wheat" is literally "wheat of strokes." He suggests a reading that makes the verse agree with 1 Kings 5:11. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/2-10.htm
- JFB sees no contradiction with 1 Kings 5:11. The yearly supplies in Kings went to Huram's court, while these went to the workmen. Gill: payment came as food because Tyre depended on Israel for wheat (Acts 12:20). Cambridge: the meaning of "beaten wheat" is uncertain, and a cor is about 394 litres. Benson: employers should see that workers are both paid and well fed. Same URL.
- Precept Austin, quoting Dillard: Tyre needed imported food. That comes to roughly 125,000 bushels each of wheat and barley, though the exact measures are uncertain. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-2-commentary
- The BibleHub study page links this verse to "the worker is worthy of his wages" (Luke 10:7). https://biblehub.com/2_chronicles/2-10.htm

**vv. 11–12**
- Matthew Henry: a wise and godly king is a sign of God's special love for his people. He points ahead to God's greater love in giving his Son. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_chronicles/2.htm
- Guzik: we cannot know whether Hiram was a true believer, but he respected Israel's God, probably because of David's influence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-2/
- Preacher's Homiletical, citing the Speaker's Commentary: several Asian nations used "who made heaven and earth" as a title for their supreme god. Hiram's friendship with father and son is also drawn on as a lesson about loyalty to old friends. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/2-12.html

**vv. 13–14**
- *Huram-abi:* Barnes says the KJV wording is a mistranslation. The man is the craftsman, not the king's father, whose name was Abibaal according to the Pulpit Commentary. "Abi" is either a proper name or an honorary title such as "master workman." Gill and Poole say much the same, and Gill names Luther among those who read it as a name. Cambridge: "my father" is a title of honour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/2-13.htm
- The NET Bible note says the name means "Huram [is] my father." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/o/w/passage.php?passage=2Ch+2%3A13%2C14
- *Dan or Naphtali?* 1 Kings 7:14 calls his mother a widow of Naphtali. Coffman says she was a Danite by birth who lived in Naphtali, so there is no contradiction. Preacher's Homiletical, citing Stanley, says Jewish tradition links him to the family of Oholiab, the Danite craftsman of the tabernacle. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/2-12.html

**v. 15**
- Precept Austin: this was a business deal, not a request for a handout. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64185/

**vv. 17–18**
- Ellicott: the "strangers" were the local Canaanite people, and the numbers add up to 153,600. Keil & Delitzsch: they descended from Canaanites who were never driven out. The census refers back to 1 Chronicles 22:2. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/2-17.htm
- Poole and Benson say David's count of foreigners was not done out of vanity, unlike his sinful census in 2 Samuel 24. Solomon counted again because deaths would have changed the numbers. Gill, citing Kimchi, says they were not idolaters but "proselytes of the gate." Same URL, and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/2-chronicles-2.html
- **Where commentators disagree:** Coffman (Restoration Movement) says Solomon's census was just as sinful as David's in 1 Chronicles 21, and amounted to enslaving foreigners. Matthew Henry says the workers were no doubt paid, since the law forbade oppressing a stranger. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/2-17.html
- Guzik: through these foreign workers the nations literally helped build the temple. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-2/

**Not found:**
- v. 16 (rafts to Joppa): no commentary beyond Guzik restating the verse.
- Protestant tradition differences: the Coffman/Henry split above is a difference between individual commentators, not between traditions.
- Catholic and Orthodox readings.
- bibleodyssey.org: nothing found. The only modern-scholarship notes are the NET note on Huram-abi and the remarks quoted from Selman and Dillard.
